extracted.intended_audience: general news readers and media observers (people interested in media ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and informal standards about borrowing, attributing, and correcting sourced material in newspaper opinion columns, illustrated by the Maureen Dowd/Josh Marshall episode. Covers what is acceptable to quote, what counts as problematic copying, and how to handle corrections and attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable quoting with attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: To better illustrate a point or a thought when writing a column, article, or blog it goes without saying that it's commonplace and perfectly acceptable to quote someone or some source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting others is a standard and acceptable practice when used to illustrate or strengthen an argument; such quotes should be clearly attributed to their source. Example: authors commonly improve their pieces by using other people's words—but they should be cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid copying others' words without attribution (avoid plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an axiom of the new digital media age that high-profile political columnists should generally avoid copying other people's words without attribution. Nobody wants to have the p-word hung around their necks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unattributed borrowing of phrasing or passages is unacceptable and risks charges of plagiarism. Even if the borrowing seems minor, failing to attribute can damage credibility, especially for prominent columnists. Anti-pattern: lifting paragraphs verbatim without acknowledging the original writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify provenance of borrowed material (due diligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a columnist is to borrow a paragraph unattributed, then at least they should ensure it doesn't belong to Josh Marshall. The man behind Talking Points Memo is one of the sharpest, most deadly bloggers around.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before using material reported to have come from a friend or informal source, verify whether the wording or idea originates elsewhere. Relying on a recollection from a third party without checking can result in unintentionally repeating someone else's work. Anti-patterns include accepting a friend's verbatim recall as original without checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt correction and transparent acknowledgement of errors
rubrics_metrics.description: "Maureen had us correct the column online as soon as the error was brought to her attention, adding in the sourcing to Marshall's blog. We ran a correction in today's paper, referring readers to the correct version online."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an attribution error is discovered, correct the online version quickly and run a print correction where appropriate. Publicly acknowledge the mistake and indicate the fix so readers know the record has been set straight. This reduces harm to reputation and maintains transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute use of feeds, staff reporting, freelancers, and conversational lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists often use feeds from other staff journalists, free-lancers, stringers, a whole range of people. And from friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard newsroom practice includes using others' reporting and informal contributions, but those sources should be credited as appropriate. If using material that originated through feeds or informal conversations, indicate the source or context to avoid confusion about originality. Examples: cite staff reporting, name freelancers, note when a line came from a conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistency between criticism and personal practice (avoid hypocrisy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because this is Dowd, the high liberal priestess of biting political criticism, the woman who excoriated Joe Biden for plagiarism, her crime is further stained by an air of hypocrisy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Columnists who publicly criticize others for ethical lapses (e.g., plagiarism) should be especially careful to follow the standards they endorse. Failure to do so amplifies negative reaction and undermines credibility. Scoring note: perceived hypocrisy often worsens public response beyond the initial error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for inadvertent borrowing and follow-up communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Dowd claims this was an accident, and that she got the idea for the material in question while chatting with a friend. Yes, it's odd that her 'friend' recalled Marshall's article verbatim, but that's Dowd's story and she's sticking to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if borrowing is inadvertent, the writer is responsible for the final text and should answer follow-up inquiries and correct the record. Not responding to queries or failing to explain the sourcing can exacerbate the issue. Example anti-patterns: ignoring emails asking about sourcing; relying on improbable explanations without evidence.
